t24.text: Graph a function by determining local maxima and minima and points of inflection, horizontal and non-horizontal, considering any even or odd symmetry, the domain, any vertical asymptotes or other discontinuities, and where applicable, the behaviour of a function as x→± ∞
Use the second derivative to classify a stationary point as a local maximum, local minimum or a horizontal point of inflection
Define a point of inflection on a curve as a point where the concavity changes

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -x^3 + 3x^2 - 1 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -3x^2 + 6x \\ &= 3x(2 - x) \end{aligned}$$
When $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, we have $3x(2-x) = 0$.
$$x = 0, \qquad x = 2$$
$$y = -1 \qquad y = -2^3 + 3(2)^2 - 1 = 3$$
Stationary points are $(0, -1)$ and $(2, 3)$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -6x + 6$$
When $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$, we have $6(1-x) = 0$.
$$x = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -1^3 + 3\times 1^2 - 1 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The point of inflection is $(1, 1)$.

\exfigure{33_q16_1}

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 2y + 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\times 2\pi x \\ &= 2\left(\dfrac{36}{x} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x\right) + 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x \\ &= \dfrac{72}{x} - \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x + 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x \\ &= 2x + \dfrac{72}{x} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 2 - \dfrac{72}{x^2}$$

$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2} = \dfrac{144}{6^3} \text{ which is greater than zero.}$$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= c\ln x \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{c}{x} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x = p$ is $\dfrac{c}{p}$.

At $x = p$, $y = c\ln p$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}(x - p) \\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c \\ y &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c + c\ln p \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{c}{p} = 1 \quad (\text{since the tangent has a gradient of } 1)$$
$$\therefore\ c = p$$
$$-c + c\ln p = 0 \quad (\text{since the tangent passes through the origin})$$
$$\begin{aligned} -c + c\ln c &= 0 \\ c(-1 + \ln c) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$c = 0 \text{ or } \ln c = 1$$
$$\therefore\ c = e \quad (\text{as } c > 0)$$
criteria: States that $\dfrac{c}{p} = 1$ or $-c + c\ln p = 0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Read each value from the graph:

$x = -2$ is a local minimum, so the curve is concave up there: $f''(-2) > 0$.

$x = 3$ is a stationary point: $f'(3) = 0$.

The curve is below the $x$-axis at $x = 0$: $f(0) < 0$.

$$\therefore\ f(0) < f'(3) < f''(-2)$$

Both ends of the graph go down, so the quartic has a negative leading coefficient.

$y = (x+1)(2-x)^3$ has roots $-1$ and $2$ (triple), and its leading term is $x\cdot(-x)^3 = -x^4$, which is negative.

parts.latex:
Let $h(x)=f(g(x))$ where the function $f(x)$ is an odd function and the function $g(x)$ is an even function.

t24.text: Solve problems involving even and odd functions
Develop and use the tests that a function f(x) is odd if f( ―x)= ―f(x) and a function f(x) is even if f( ―x)= f(x)

solutions.latex:
$g$ is even, so $h(-x) = f\big(g(-x)\big) = f\big(g(x)\big) = h(x)$: $h$ is an even function.

The graph of an even function is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so
$$h(-k) = h(k) = mk + c \qquad\text{and}\qquad h'(-k) = -h'(k) = -m$$
Tangent at $x = -k$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - (mk + c) &= -m(x + k) \\ y &= -mx - mk + mk + c \\ y &= -mx + c \end{aligned}$$

t24.text: Solve problems involving equations of tangents and normals to curves involving any of the functions within the scope of the Mathematics Advanced course

solutions.latex:
The tangent passes through the origin and the point $(a, \cos a)$, so
$$m = \dfrac{\cos a}{a}$$
From the diagram $\cos a < 1$, so $m < \dfrac{1}{a}$.

At $x = 2\pi$ the curve has $\cos 2\pi = 1$. The tangent touches the curve where it is concave down, so near the peak at $2\pi$ the line lies above the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} m(2\pi) &> 1 \\ m &> \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{2\pi} < m < \dfrac{1}{a}$$

solutions.latex:
$$P = 5000b^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
When $t = 20$, $P = 1250$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1250 &= 5000\,b^{-2} \\ b^{-2} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ b &= 2 \quad (b > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 5000(2)^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 5000\times\ln 2\times\dfrac{-1}{10}\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}}$$
Find $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -30$:
$$\begin{aligned} -30 &= -500\times\ln 2\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{500\ln 2}{30} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= 11.55\ldots \\ \dfrac{t}{10}\ln 2 &= \ln 11.55\ldots \\ t &= 35.3 \end{aligned}$$

Let $c > 0$ be the $x$-value of the vertical asymptote of $y = g(x)$.

$g(f(x))$ is undefined where $f(x) = x^2 = c$, so it has vertical asymptotes at $x = \pm\sqrt{c}$. $f$ is even, so $g(f(x))$ is even: the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= k(x - m)^2 - 5 \\ &= k\left(x^2 - 2xm + m^2\right) - 5 \\ &= kx^2 - 2mkx + m^2k - 5 \end{aligned}$$
By inspection $k = 3$.

By equating coefficient of $x$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2mk &= 12 \\ 6m &= 12 \\ m &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

So $k = 3$ and $m = 2$.

$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ for } 0 < x < \pi$$

solutions.latex:
We need $F\left(e^3\right) = 1$, since $F(x)$ is a CDF.
$$\begin{aligned} F\left(e^3\right) &= \dfrac{1}{k}\ln e^3 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{k} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{3}{k} = 1$.
$$\therefore\ k = 3$$

$$P(X > c) = 1 - P(X < c)$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} P(X < c) &= 2\left[1 - P(X < c)\right] \\ 3P(X < c) &= 2 \\ P(X < c) &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(c) = \dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\ln c &= \dfrac{2}{3} \\ \ln c &= 2 \\ c &= e^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises that $P(X > c) = 1 - P(X < c)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The shaded region between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ is below the $x$-axis with area $1$:
$$\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = -1$$
$f$ is odd, so $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0$, and
$$\int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx = \int_{-a}^{0} f(x)\,dx + \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx = 0 + (-1) = -1$$

We want the equation $e^{-2x}=e^{-x}+k$ to have 2 solutions.

$$e^{-x}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4k}}{2}$$
For two real solutions we want $1+4k>0$, i.e. $k>-\dfrac{1}{4}$.

But for two solutions for $e^{-x}$, both the real solutions to the quadratic must be positive.
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \sqrt{1+4k}&<1\\\therefore\ 1+4k&<1\\\therefore\ k&<0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{1}{4}<k<0$$
criteria: Uses the discriminant to find $k>-\dfrac{1}{4}$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to form a quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2x\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
which increases on $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (sketch).

$\therefore\ \alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x) = uv$ with $u = x$, $u' = 1$, $v = e^{-x^2}$, $v' = -2xe^{-x^2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= x\left(-2xe^{-x^2}\right) + e^{-x^2} \\ &= (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} &= 0 \\ 1 - 2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ x &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \text{ or } x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
When $x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
$\therefore$ The stationary points are
$$\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$
and
$$\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$

parts.latex:
The lamp shown in the diagram below can move along the vertical line $OB$ using a pulley system. The point $A$ lies on the horizontal line $OA$ at a distance of $d$ from $O$. The intensity $I$ of light from the lamp at point $A$ is inversely proportional to the square of its distance $r$ from the lamp. The intensity $I$ is also directly proportional to $\sin\phi$, where $\phi$ is the angle of elevation from $A$ to the lamp. Hence, the formula for $I$ can be expressed as:
$$I=\dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}, \quad \text{where } C \text{ is a positive constant.}$$
Determine the height $h$ of the lamp above the line $OA$ that maximizes the intensity of light at the point $A$. Express your answer in terms of $d$.

\exfigure{408_q31_1}

t24.text: Solve optimisation problems by using calculus to find local and global maxima and minima of differentiable functions, checking discontinuities of f'(x) and endpoints of the domain if applicable

figures.cap: lamp at B above O, right triangle OAB with height h, base d, hypotenuse r, angle phi at A

solutions.latex:
The lamp is $h$ above $O$ and $A$ is $d$ from $O$, so $O$, $A$ and the lamp form a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $r$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$r^2 = h^2 + d^2$$
$\phi$ is the angle at $A$, and the side opposite it is $h$:
$$\sin\phi = \dfrac{h}{r} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}$$
Substitute both into $I = \dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}$ to write $I$ in terms of $h$ only:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= C\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{h^2+d^2}\right) \\ &= Ch(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate using the product rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dh} &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} + Ch\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)(2h)(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}} \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}\left[(h^2+d^2) - 3h^2\right] \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}(d^2 - 2h^2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $C>0$ and $(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}>0$, $\dfrac{dI}{dh}=0$ when
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 - 2h^2 &= 0 \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} \\ h &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d \quad (h>0) \end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dI}{dh}$ is the sign of $d^2-2h^2$. Test either side:
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{d}{2}: & d^2-2\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} > 0 \\ h &= d: & d^2-2d^2 &= -d^2 < 0 \end{aligned}$$
$I$ increases then decreases, so the stationary point is a maximum.

$\therefore$ The intensity at $A$ is greatest when $h = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d$.
criteria: Makes a suitable substitution, $\sin\phi=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\int_{-\log_3 b}^{0} \left(-3^{-x} + b\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{\ln 3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left[\dfrac{3^{-x}}{\ln 3} + bx\right]_{-\log_3 b}^{0} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} + 0\right) - \left(\dfrac{3^{\log_3 b}}{\ln 3} - b\log_3 b\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b \end{aligned}$$
LHS = RHS:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ -\dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b &= 0 \\ b\log_3 b &= \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} \end{aligned}$$
Since $b \ne 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_3 b &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ \dfrac{\ln b}{\ln 3} &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ \ln b &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b = e$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{2^n-2^{n-1}}{2^{n+1}+2^n}$?

solutions.latex:
In 6 hours the bricklayer lays
$$\dfrac{6\times 60\times 60}{10} = 2160 \text{ bricks}$$
The rows form an arithmetic series with $a = 150$ and $d = -3$:
$$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2\times 150 + (n-1)(-3)\big) = \dfrac{n}{2}(303 - 3n)$$
$$\begin{aligned} S_{17} &= \dfrac{17}{2}(303 - 51) = 2142 \le 2160 \\ S_{18} &= 9(303 - 54) = 2241 > 2160 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For what values of $b$ is the function $y=x^4+bx^3-3x^2$ concave up and decreasing at the point where $x=1$?

t24.text: Interpret the second derivative y'' as the gradient function of the first derivative y', and deduce that if y'' > 0 the curve is concave up and if y'' < 0 the curve is concave down

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 4x^3 + 3bx^2 - 6x \\ y'' &= 12x^2 + 6bx - 6 \end{aligned}$$
Decreasing at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 + 3b - 6 &< 0 \\ b &< \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Concave up at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12 + 6b - 6 &> 0 \\ b &> -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -1 < b < \dfrac{2}{3}, \text{ that is } b \in \left(-1, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$$

parts.latex:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line such that its acceleration with respect to time is given by $a=-2t+3$, where $a$ is the acceleration of the particle at time $t$ seconds for $t\ge 0$.

The particle is at rest when $t=1$ and $t=2$.

Which of the following graphs best represents the displacement of the particle?

t24.text: Solve problems relating to the motion of a particle moving in a straight line, using both differentiation and integration to connect the concepts of displacement, velocity and acceleration
Use integration to solve practical problems on the rate of change of a quantity Q, where dQ dt or d2Q dt2 is given as a function of time t, together with sufficient initial conditions

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$v = \int(-2t+3)\,dt = -t^2 + 3t + C$$
The particle is at rest at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, so $v = 0$ there:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 + 3 + C &= 0 \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$v = -t^2 + 3t - 2 = -(t-1)(t-2)$$
Sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &< 0 &&\text{for } 0 \le t < 1 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\\ v &> 0 &&\text{for } 1 < t < 2 &&\text{displacement increasing}\\ v &< 0 &&\text{for } t > 2 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the displacement has a local minimum at $t = 1$ and a local maximum at $t = 2$.

Graph A is the only graph with a minimum at $t = 1$, a maximum at $t = 2$ and decreasing afterwards. (Graph B has the turning points the wrong way round; C and D do not have stationary points at both $t = 1$ and $t = 2$.)

The amount of fuel, $F(t)$ litres, consumed at time $t$ hours is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int R\,dt \\ &= \int 5+4e^{-0.5t}\,dt \\ &= 5t-8e^{-0.5t}+c \end{aligned}$$

t24.text: Use the Trapezoidal rule to approximate integrals

figures.cap: curve y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4 with trapezia, heights 4, 5.125, 13

solutions.latex:
Exact area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75 \end{aligned}$$

Two applications of the trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$ means two strips, each of width
$$h=\dfrac{3-0}{2}=1.5$$
so the function values are needed at $x=0,\ 1.5,\ 3$:
$$f(0)=4,\qquad f(1.5)=5.125,\qquad f(3)=13$$
Estimate using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13] \\ &\approx 20.4375 \end{aligned}$$

$$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$

$\therefore$ The trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by $1.6875 \text{ units}^2$.
criteria: Finds the area using integration and the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
Finds the area using either the trapezoidal rule or integration, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

The height after the $n$th bounce is the $n$th term of the geometric progression with first term $a=\dfrac{qH}{100}$ (the first rebound) and common ratio $r=\dfrac{q}{100}$, $0<q<100$.

Total distance travelled may be modelled as the limiting sum of a geometric series, since $0<r<1$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= H+2(h_1+h_2+h_3+\cdots) \\ &= H+2\left(\dfrac{\frac{qH}{100}}{1-\frac{q}{100}}\right) \\ &= H+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100-q)}{100-q}+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H-qH+2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H+qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q} \end{aligned}$$

Maximise the volume by maximising the area of the cross-section, since the depth is constant.

Let $A$ be the area of the cross-section of the tent.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 5x\times h \\ &= 5xy+\dfrac{5xh}{2} \end{aligned}$$

From parts (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5x(10-4x)+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-20x^2+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x^2 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating $y=x^3-2x$ with $y=x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-2x &= x^2 \\ x^3-x^2-2x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-x-2) &= 0 \\ x(x+1)(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Hence the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $-1$ and the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is $2$.

Area between the two curves is given by
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_{-1}^{0}x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_0^2 x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right| \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|+\left|4-\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{12} \end{aligned}$$

It is known that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. (Do NOT prove this.)

t24.text: Establish and use ∫u' u dx = ln|u| + C, where u is a function of x, or ∫f'(x) f(x) dx = ln |f(x)| + C, on a domain where f(x)≠0

solutions.latex:
Divide the numerator and denominator of the integrand by $x^2$ such that:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{x\ln x}{x^2}}\,dx \\ &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx \end{aligned}$$

Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$$
and
$$\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$$

$$\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx\text{ is in the form }\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$$

Hence,
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \ln\left|\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right|+c \\ &= \ln|\ln x|-\ln|x|+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes substantial progress toward correct solution, such as recognising that the integral is in the form $\displaystyle \int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and hence will result in a log function by using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Product rule with $u = 2x$, $v = e^{-x}$: $u' = 2$, $v' = -e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2e^{-x} + 2x(-e^{-x}) \\ &= 2e^{-x} - 2xe^{-x} \\ &= 2e^{-x}(1-x) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$.

Since $2e^{-x} > 0$ for all $x$, we need $1 - x = 0$, so $x = 1$.

$f(1) = 2e^{-1} = \dfrac{2}{e}$.

Nature:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= -2e^{-x}(1-x) - 2e^{-x} \\ &= 2e^{-x}(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$f''(1) = 2e^{-1}(-1) = -\dfrac{2}{e} < 0$, so the curve is concave down there.

$\therefore$ $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.
criteria: Finds $x=1$ and the stationary point $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$f(x) = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$. As $x \to \infty$, $e^x$ grows much faster than $2x$, so
$$\lim_{x \to \infty} 2xe^{-x} = 0$$

$f''(x) = 2e^{-x}(x-2)$.

Since $2e^{-x} > 0$, $f''(x) = 0$ only when $x = 2$.

Check the change in concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(1) &= -2e^{-1} < 0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(3) &= 2e^{-3} > 0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The sign changes, so it is a point of inflection.
$$f(2) = 4e^{-2}$$
$\therefore$ The point of inflection is $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
$$x = \int 2\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)dt = -2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -2\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C \\ 0 &= -2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
At rest means $v = 0$: $\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$, so $t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 0, \pi, \dots$

$\therefore$ The first time with $t \ge 0$ is $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} v(0) &= 2\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 2\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= -\sqrt{3} \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

Since $-1 \le \sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \le 1$, we have $-2 \le v \le 2$.

$\therefore$ The maximum speed is $|v|_{\max} = 2$ m/s. (It occurs, for example, at $t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.)

$v = 2\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is the graph of $y = 2\sin t$ shifted $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the right. It has amplitude $2$ and period $2\pi$.

\exfigure{568_q15_s1}
criteria: Shows the intercepts $(0,-\sqrt{3})$, $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit
Draws the correct shape (shifted sine, amplitude $2$) over $[0,2\pi]$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so split the time interval there. Using $x = 1 - 2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ from (i):
$$x(0) = 0, \qquad x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1 - 2\cos 0 = -1, \qquad x(\pi) = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = 1 + 1 = 2$$
Distance for $0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{3}$: $|-1 - 0| = 1$ m.

Distance for $\dfrac{\pi}{3} \le t \le \pi$: $|2 - (-1)| = 3$ m.

$\therefore$ Total distance $= 1 + 3 = 4$ m.

figures.cap: isosceles trapezium ABCD inscribed in semicircle centre O, diameter AD = 20 cm, perpendiculars BE and CF, EO = OF = x/2

solutions.latex:
$O$ is the centre and the diameter is $20$ cm, so $OB = 10$ cm (radius).

In right-angled triangle $BEO$ (right angle at $E$), $EO = \dfrac{x}{2}$. By Pythagoras:
$$\begin{aligned} BE^2 &= OB^2 - EO^2 \\ &= 100 - \dfrac{x^2}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{400 - x^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BE = \dfrac{\sqrt{400 - x^2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{400 - x^2}$$
criteria: Uses $OB=10$ (radius) and Pythagoras in triangle $BEO$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$BCFE$ is a rectangle, so $BC = EF = EO + OF = x$. The parallel sides are $AD = 20$ and $BC = x$, and the height is $BE$.

Area of a trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(AD + BC)\times BE \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(20 + x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{400 - x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}(x + 20)\sqrt{400 - x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses $BC=x$ and finds the height $BE$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Substitute into the trapezium area formula
meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
Product rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\sqrt{400 - x^2} + (x + 20)\cdot\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{400 - x^2}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{400 - x^2 - x^2 - 20x}{4\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-2(x^2 + 10x - 200)}{4\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \\ &= -\dfrac{(x + 20)(x - 10)}{2\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$: since $0 < x < 20$, $x + 20 \neq 0$, so $x = 10$.

Nature:
$$\begin{aligned} x &< 10 &&\text{(just below)}: & \dfrac{dA}{dx} &> 0\\ x &> 10 &&\text{(just above)}: & \dfrac{dA}{dx} &< 0\end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ changes from $+$ to $-$, so $x = 10$ gives a maximum.

$\therefore$ Since $BC = x$, the area is maximised when $BC = 10$ cm. (The maximum area is $75\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2$.)
criteria: Finds and simplifies $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} &= 16 \times 0.90 \\ &= 14.4 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

$$S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r} = \dfrac{14.4}{1 - 0.9} = 144 \text{ hours}$$
The battery will last
$$\begin{aligned} &= 25 + 20 + 16 + 144 \\ &= 205 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
$T_n < 1$, $n = ?$
$$\begin{aligned} 14.4 \times 0.9^{n-1} &< 1 \\ 0.9^{n-1} &< \dfrac{1}{14.4} \end{aligned}$$
Taking logs of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} (n-1)\log 0.9 &< \log\left(\dfrac{1}{14.4}\right) \\ n - 1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{1}{14.4}\right)}{\log 0.9} \\ n &> 25.3152 + 1 \\ n &> 26.3152 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} n &= 27 + 2 \text{ previous charges} \\ n &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The power is less than $1$ hour after the $29^{\text{th}}$ charge.

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 4x^3 + 3bx^2 - 6x \\ y'' &= 12x^2 + 6bx - 6 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line such that its acceleration with respect to time is given by $a=-2t+3$, where $a$ is the acceleration of the particle at time $t$ seconds for $t\ge 0$.

The particle is at rest when $t=1$ and $t=2$.

Which of the following graphs best represents the displacement of the particle?

t24.text: Solve problems relating to the motion of a particle moving in a straight line, using both differentiation and integration to connect the concepts of displacement, velocity and acceleration
Use integration to solve practical problems on the rate of change of a quantity Q, where dQ dt or d2Q dt2 is given as a function of time t, together with sufficient initial conditions

figures.cap: option A: option A: x-t graph starting at x=2, local min near t=1, local max near t=2, then decreasing
option B: option B: x-t graph starting at x=-2, local max near t=1, local min near t=2, then increasing
option C: option C: concave-down parabola starting at x=-2 crossing t-axis at t=1 and t=2
option D: option D: decreasing straight line crossing t-axis between 1 and 2

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$v = \int(-2t+3)\,dt = -t^2 + 3t + C$$
The particle is at rest at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, so $v = 0$ there:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 + 3 + C &= 0 \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$v = -t^2 + 3t - 2 = -(t-1)(t-2)$$
Sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &< 0 &&\text{for } 0 \le t < 1 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\\ v &> 0 &&\text{for } 1 < t < 2 &&\text{displacement increasing}\\ v &< 0 &&\text{for } t > 2 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the displacement has a local minimum at $t = 1$ and a local maximum at $t = 2$.

Graph A is the only graph with a minimum at $t = 1$, a maximum at $t = 2$ and decreasing afterwards. (Graph B has the turning points the wrong way round; C and D do not have stationary points at both $t = 1$ and $t = 2$.)

t24.text: Generate and use the formulas E(X)= μ = ΣxP(x) and Var(X)= σ2 = Σ(x ― μ)2P(x)= Σx2P(x)― μ2 for the random variable X, where Var(X) is the variance and σ is the standard deviation of the distribution

solutions.latex:
Sum of probabilities equals 1:
$$\begin{aligned}0.05+p+p+q+0.01&=1\\ 2p+q&=0.94\quad(1)\end{aligned}$$
$E(X)=2.08$:
$$\begin{aligned}(0\times 0.05)+(1\times p)+(2\times p)+(3\times q)+(4\times 0.01)&=2.08\\ 3p+3q&=2.04\\ p+q&=0.68\quad(2)\end{aligned}$$

From (1): $q=0.94-2p$.

Substitute for $q$ in (2):
$$\begin{aligned}p+0.94-2p&=0.68\\ -p&=-0.26\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ p=0.26$ and $q=0.42$

By calculating the effective annual rate of interest for both retirement funds, or otherwise, determine whether Maroun should remain with the current retirement fund or change to the alternative retirement fund.
parts.note: effective annual interest rate comparison of compound interest funds; no 2024 dot point

solutions.latex:
Balance at the end of the fourth month:
$$496994.00+1490.98-3800=494684.98$$
$\therefore$ Balance at the end of the fourth month is $\$494\,684.98$.

Interest earned at the end of the fifth month:
$$494684.98\times 0.003=1484.05$$
$\therefore$ Interest earned at the end of the fifth month is $\$1484.05$.

Amount Maroun withdrew at the end of the fifth month:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Balance} &= P+I-M \\ M &= P+I-\text{Balance} \\ &= 494684.98+1484.05-491969.03 \\ &= 4200 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Maroun withdrew $\$4200$ at the end of the fifth month.
criteria: Finds the interest earned at the end of the fifth month, or equivalent merit
Finds the balance at the end of the fourth month, or equivalent merit
Determines the balance at the end of the sixth month, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Effective annual rate of interest for the current retirement fund:
$$\begin{aligned} (1+0.003)^{12}-1 &= 0.036599\ldots \\ &\approx 3.66\%\text{ p.a.} \end{aligned}$$
Effective annual rate of interest for the alternative retirement fund:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(1+\dfrac{0.032}{365}\right)^{365}-1 &= 0.032516\ldots \\ &\approx 3.25\%\text{ p.a.} \end{aligned}$$
The effective annual rate of interest for the alternative retirement fund is less than Maroun's current retirement fund, hence Maroun should stay with his current retirement fund.

Alternatively, compare the future value (FV) of one dollar invested in both funds.

Current fund:
$$\text{FV}=(1+0.3\%)^{12}=\$1.03659998$$
Alternative fund:
$$\text{FV}=\left(1+\dfrac{3.2\%}{365}\right)^{365}=\$1.032516057$$
The FV of the alternative fund is less than the FV of the current fund, hence Maroun should stay with his current retirement fund.
criteria: Finds the effective annual rate of interest for one of the funds, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A rocket is returning back to Earth after completing a space mission.

Its distance from Earth can be modelled by the equation

$$S=55000\times 3^{-0.182t},$$

where $S$ is the distance from Earth in kilometres at time $t$ hours after it begins its return journey.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered page images (default review)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the speed of the rocket after 2 hours on its return journey.

t24.text: Prove and use the formula d dx(ax)= ( ln a )ax, where a is a constant and a > 0
Use differentiation to find and interpret the first and second derivatives, dQ dt and d2Q dt2 , in practical problems where a quantity Q is a function of time t

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
When the rocket reaches a distance of 1000 km from Earth, a parachute is released.

How long, in hours, after the rocket begins its return journey does it release its parachute? Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

t24.text: Explain that y = ax is equivalent to x = loga y for a > 0 and a ≠1, and use the equivalence to solve equations of the form ax = b, for a > 0

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(t)=\dfrac{dS}{dt} &= -0.182\times\ln 3\times 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182t} \end{aligned}$$
Speed of the rocket at time $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(2) &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182\times 2} \\ &= -7372.3576\ldots \\ \text{speed} &= |S'(2)| \approx 7372 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The speed of the rocket 2 hours after it begins its return journey is $7372 \text{ km/h}$.
criteria: Correctly differentiates to find an equation for speed, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: an absolute value was set equal to a negative number.

solutions.latex:
Let $S=1000$ and solve the equation for $t$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000 &= 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ \dfrac{1}{55} &= 3^{-0.182t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right) &= -0.182t\times\ln 3 \\ t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right)\div(-0.182\times\ln 3) \\ &= 20.0419\ldots \\ &\approx 20.04 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The rocket deploys its parachute 20.04 hours after it begins its return journey.
criteria: Attempts to solve for $t$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The graph below shows the curve $y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4$.

Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$, determine how much the Trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve. \exfigure{1346_q30_1}

t24.text: Use the Trapezoidal rule to approximate integrals

Apply ∫b a f(x) dx = F(b)― F(a), where F(x) is a primitive of f(x), to calculate definite integrals and solve related theoretical problems involving functions within the scope of the Mathematics Advanced course

figures.cap: curve y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4 with trapezium chords; heights 4 at x=0, 5.125 at x=1.5, 13 at x=3

solutions.latex:
Exact area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75 \end{aligned}$$
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$ means two strips, each of width
$$h=\dfrac{3-0}{2}=1.5$$
so the function values are needed at $x=0,\ 1.5,\ 3$:
$$f(0)=4,\qquad f(1.5)=5.125,\qquad f(3)=13$$
Estimate using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13] \\ &\approx 20.4375 \end{aligned}$$
$$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$
$\therefore$ The trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by $1.6875 \text{ units}^2$.
criteria: Finds the area using integration and the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
Finds the area using either the trapezoidal rule or integration, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A ball is dropped from a height $H$ metres above the ground. Each time it strikes the ground, it rebounds to a lower height which is $q\%$ of its previous height.

Let $h_n$ be the height reached by the ball after the $n$th bounce.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered page images (default review)

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that, after the second bounce, the ball rebounds to a height given by

$$h_2=\dfrac{q^2H}{(100)^2}.$$

t24.text: Develop the formula an = arn―1 for the nth term of a GP, where a is the first term and n ≥1, and use it to solve problems
Apply the formulas for geometric sequences and series to model and solve growth and decay problems where a quantity is an exponential function of time

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the total distance, $D$, travelled by the ball is given by

$$D=\dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q}.$$

t24.text: Develop the formula S∞= a 1―r for the limiting sum of a geometric series with |r|< 1, and use this formula to solve problems
Apply the formulas for geometric sequences and series to model and solve growth and decay problems where a quantity is an exponential function of time

solutions.latex:
Initial height of the ball is $H$ metres.

The height after the $n$th bounce is the $n$th term of the geometric progression with first term $a=\dfrac{qH}{100}$ (the first rebound) and common ratio $r=\dfrac{q}{100}$, $0<q<100$.

Height after the second bounce:
$$\begin{aligned} h_n &= T_n=ar^{n-1} \\ h_2 &= \dfrac{qH}{100}\times\dfrac{q}{100} \\ &= \dfrac{q^2H}{(100)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to model height of bounce as a geometric progression, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the first term was given as $H$, which would make $h_2=\dfrac{qH}{100}$.

solutions.latex:
Total distance travelled may be modelled as the limiting sum of a geometric series, since $0<r<1$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= H+2(h_1+h_2+h_3+\cdots) \\ &= H+2\left(\dfrac{\frac{qH}{100}}{1-\frac{q}{100}}\right) \\ &= H+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100-q)}{100-q}+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H-qH+2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H+qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to simplify the expression involving the limiting sum, or equivalent merit
Correctly models the total distance involving the limiting sum, or equivalent merit

Maximise the volume by maximising the area of the cross-section, since the depth is constant.

Let $A$ be the area of the cross-section of the tent.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 5x\times h \\ &= 5xy+\dfrac{5xh}{2} \end{aligned}$$
From parts (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5x(10-4x)+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-20x^2+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=50-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x$$

The diagram shows the graphs of $y=x^3-2x$ and $y=x^2$. \exfigure{1346_q33_1} The graphs intersect at $A$, $B$ and the origin, $O$.

By finding the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, show that the area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{37}{12}$.

t24.text: Use definite integrals to solve problems involving the areas of regions bounded by the graph of the continuous function y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b, in cases where f(x)≥0 throughout a ≤x ≤b, f(x)≤0 throughout a ≤x ≤b or where f(x) changes sign in the interval a ≤x ≤b, with or without the graph provided

parts.note: area between two curves: examinable (confirmed by Steve)

figures.cap: graphs of y=x^3-2x and y=x^2 intersecting at A, O, B with the two enclosed regions shaded

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating $y=x^3-2x$ with $y=x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-2x &= x^2 \\ x^3-x^2-2x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-x-2) &= 0 \\ x(x+1)(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $-1$ and the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is $2$.

Area between the two curves is given by
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_{-1}^{0}x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_0^2 x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right| \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|+\left|4-\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly sets up a sum of two integrals, including correct bounds for each integral, and attempts to find the area between the two curves, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
It is known that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx$.

t24.text: Establish and use ∫u' u dx = ln|u| + C, where u is a function of x, or ∫f'(x) f(x) dx = ln |f(x)| + C, on a domain where f(x)≠0

solutions.latex:
Divide the numerator and denominator of the integrand by $x^2$ such that:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{x\ln x}{x^2}}\,dx \\ &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx \end{aligned}$$
Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$$
and
$$\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$$

$$\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx\text{ is in the form }\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$$
Hence,
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \ln\left|\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right|+c \\ &= \ln|\ln x|-\ln|x|+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes substantial progress toward correct solution, such as recognising that the integral is in the form $\displaystyle \int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and hence will result in a log function by using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$, or equivalent merit

t24.text: Develop the formula Sn = a(1―rn) 1―r for the sum of the first n terms of a GP where r ≠1, and use this formula to solve problems

solutions.latex:
$GP_1=1+2+4+8+\cdots$, with $a_1=1$, $r_1=2$.

$$GP_2=\dfrac13+\dfrac19+\dfrac1{27}+\dfrac1{81}+\cdots$$
with $a_2=\dfrac13$, $r_2=\dfrac13$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a_1r_1^{n-1}+a_2r_2^{n-1} \\ &= 1(2)^{n-1}+\dfrac13\left(\dfrac13\right)^{n-1} \\ &= 2^{n-1}+\dfrac{1}{3^n} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises two separate geometric progressions, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1}+\dfrac{a_2(1-r^n)}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1(2^n-1)}{2-1}+\dfrac{\frac13\left(1-\frac{1}{3^n}\right)}{1-\frac13} \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_n=2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \text{ or } \dfrac{2^{n+1}-3^{-n}-1}{2}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{(e^x+1)-e^xx}{(e^x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(1-x)+1}{(e^x+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(1)=\dfrac{1}{(e+1)^2}$$
$$m_{\text{normal}}=-(e+1)^2$$
$$f(1)=\dfrac{1}{e+1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(x-1) \\ (e+1)y-1 &= -(e+1)^3x+(e+1)^3 \\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-(1+(e+1)^3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(1)+c \\ c &= \dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=-(e+1)^2x+\dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2$$
$$\therefore\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-1-(e+1)^3=0$$

solutions.latex:
In the cross-section, the triangle above the prism (height $H-h$, base $\dfrac{x}{2}$) is similar to the whole right-angled triangle (height $H$, base $R$): common angle at the apex, both right-angled (equiangular).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{H-h}{H} &= \dfrac{\frac{x}{2}}{R} \\ x &= 2R\left(\dfrac{H-h}{H}\right) \\ &= 2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right) \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Be careful that the correct ratio is used.
meta.top_criterion_original: Correct ratio. Do NOT need any geometric reasoning
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the question named the radius $r$ but part (a) and this working use $R$; the question now says $R$.
meta.explained: Similar-triangle reasoning explained in words (owner request, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= x^2h \\ &= \left(2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\right)^2h \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)^2 \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{H}+\dfrac{h^2}{H^2}\right) \\ &= 4R^2h-\dfrac{8R^2h^2}{H}+\dfrac{4R^2h^3}{H^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dh}=4R^2-\dfrac{16R^2h}{H}+\dfrac{12R^2h^2}{H^2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{4h}{H}+\dfrac{3h^2}{H^2}\right) &= 0 \\ 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{3h}{H}\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=H \text{ or } h=\dfrac{H}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2h}{H^2}$$
At $h=H$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=\dfrac{8R^2}{H}>0$$
$\therefore$ concave up.

At $h=\dfrac{H}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2} &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2(\frac{H}{3})}{H^2} \\ &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{8R^2}{H} \\ &= -\dfrac{8R^2}{H}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ concave down.

$\therefore\ h=\dfrac{H}{3}$ is a maximum.
criteria: Finds $V$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A probability distribution is said to have a \textbf{memoryless property} if the probability of some future event occurring is not affected by the occurrence of past events.

In formal statistic terms, a random variable $X$ is said to follow a probability distribution with a memoryless property if for any $a, x \ge 0$ it is true that:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$
